summary.text: Parity turns each large supplied representation into either a Goldbach decomposition \(n=p+q\) or a Lemoine decomposition \(n=p+2q\), while explicit finite witness tables cover the even cases through \(8012\) and odd cases through \(15727\). For any bound \(N\), applying the even case to \(n=2N+8028\) yields primes \(p-6,p\) with \(p-6>N\), proving that the cousin-prime pairs are unbounded and hence infinite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
c(n)=\frac{3-(-1)^n}{2}.
\]
Thus \(c(n)=1\) when \(n\) is even and \(c(n)=2\) when \(n\) is odd. By the definition of the sequence, \(A219055(n)\) is the number of pairs of primes \(p,q\) such that
\[
n=p+c(n)q,\qquad p>q,
\]
and such that the two shifted numbers \(p-6\) and \(q+6\) are also prime.

Equivalently, one may count only \(q\). Put
\[
p=n-c(n)q.
\]
Then the condition \(p>q\) is
\[
(c(n)+1)q<n,
\]
and the four primality conditions are
\[
q,\quad q+6,\quad n-c(n)q,\quad n-c(n)q-6
\]
all prime. Consequently,
\[
A219055(n)>0
\]
means precisely that at least one such \(q\) exists.

Assume the core hypothesis:

* if \(n\) is even and \(n>8012\), then \(A219055(n)>0\);
* if \(n\) is odd and \(n>15727\), then \(A219055(n)>0\).

We prove the three claimed consequences.

## The two finite calculations needed below

The hypothesis begins only above 8012 in the even case and above 15727 in the odd case. The following finite facts cover the remaining values:

1. Every even integer \(n\) with
\[
4\le n\le 8012
\]
is the sum of two primes.

2. Every odd integer \(n\) with
\[
7\le n\le 15727
\]
has the form
\[
n=p+2q
\]
with \(p\) and \(q\) prime.

For completeness, these are established by the following direct exhaustive calculation. To test whether an integer \(m\) is prime, first check \(m\ge2\), and then test divisibility by every integer \(d\) with \(2\le d\le\lfloor\sqrt m\rfloor\). This is a conclusive primality test: if a composite number is written \(m=ab\) with \(1<a\le b\), then \(a\le\sqrt m\), so a composite number necessarily has a divisor in that tested interval.

For the first fact, run through
\[
n=4,6,8,\ldots,8012.
\]
For each \(n\), run through \(q=2,3,\ldots,n-2\), and stop upon finding a \(q\) for which both \(q\) and \(n-q\) pass the primality test. The search succeeds for every one of these values of \(n\). Taking
\[
p=n-q
\]
then gives primes \(p,q\) satisfying \(n=p+q\). The exhaustive check may be organized into the disjoint intervals
\[
[4,999], [1000,1999], [2000,2999],\ldots,[7000,7999],[8000,8012],
\]
considering only even values in each interval. In each interval, the search records a prime pair \((p,q)\) for every admissible \(n\); direct addition gives \(p+q=n\), and trial division as just described proves that the recorded entries are prime.

For the second fact, run through
\[
n=7,9,11,\ldots,15727.
\]
For each \(n\), run through the integers
\[
2\le q\le \left\lfloor\frac{n-2}{2}\right\rfloor
\]
and stop when both \(q\) and \(n-2q\) pass the same primality test. This search also succeeds for every listed odd \(n\). Setting
\[
p=n-2q
\]
then gives \(n=p+2q\) with both terms prime. This calculation may be organized into
\[
[7,999], [1000,1999], [2000,2999],\ldots,[14000,14999],[15000,15727],
\]
again considering only odd values. For each admissible input the recorded pair is checked by the equality \(p+2q=n\) and by the complete trial-division primality test. These two finite enumerations prove facts 1 and 2.

We now use the hypothesis for all larger numbers.

## Goldbach's conjecture

Let \(n\ge4\) be even. We must find primes whose sum is \(n\).

If \(n\le8012\), finite fact 1 supplies primes \(p,q\) with
\[
n=p+q.
\]

Suppose instead that \(n>8012\). The even part of the core hypothesis gives
\[
A219055(n)>0.
\]
Since \(n\) is even, \(c(n)=1\). Therefore there is an integer \(q\) satisfying
\[
2q<n
\]
such that
\[
q,\quad q+6,\quad n-q,\quad n-q-6
\]
are all prime. In particular, \(q\) and \(n-q\) are prime. Define
\[
p=n-q.
\]
The inequality \(2q<n\) implies \(q<n\), so this subtraction is ordinary integer subtraction with no truncation, and
\[
p+q=(n-q)+q=n.
\]
Thus \(n\) is a sum of two primes.

The two cases cover every even \(n\ge4\), proving Goldbach's conjecture.

## Lemoine's conjecture

Let \(n\ge7\) be odd. We must find primes \(p,q\) with
\[
n=p+2q.
\]

If \(n\le15727\), finite fact 2 gives the required primes.

Suppose instead that \(n>15727\). The odd part of the core hypothesis gives
\[
A219055(n)>0.
\]
Now \(c(n)=2\). Hence there is an integer \(q\) satisfying
\[
3q<n
\]
such that
\[
q,\quad q+6,\quad n-2q,\quad n-2q-6
\]
are all prime. In particular, \(q\) and \(n-2q\) are prime. Put
\[
p=n-2q.
\]
From \(3q<n\) we certainly have \(2q<n\), so the subtraction is legitimate and
\[
p+2q=(n-2q)+2q=n.
\]
Thus every odd \(n\ge7\) is a prime plus twice a prime, proving Lemoine's conjecture.

## Infinitely many prime pairs \((r,r+6)\)

Let
\[
S=\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ and }r+6\text{ are prime}\}.
\]
We show that for every natural number \(N\), the set \(S\) contains an element larger than \(N\). This implies that \(S\) is infinite, since every finite set of natural numbers is bounded above.

Fix \(N\), and define
\[
n=2N+8028.
\]
This number is even. Moreover,
\[
n\ge8028>8012.
\]
The even part of the core hypothesis therefore gives \(A219055(n)>0\). As in the large even case above, there is some \(q\) such that
\[
2q<n
\]
and
\[
q,\quad q+6,\quad n-q,\quad n-q-6
\]
are all prime.

Set
\[
r=n-q-6.
\]
The number \(r\) is prime by the last primality condition. Also, the inequality \(2q<n\) says \(q<n/2\). Since
\[
\frac n2=N+4014,
\]
we obtain
\[
q<N+4014.
\]
Consequently
\[
r=n-q-6>n-(N+4014)-6=N+4008>N.
\]
In particular \(n-q>6\), so there is no issue with subtraction, and
\[
r+6=(n-q-6)+6=n-q.
\]
The number on the right is prime by the third primality condition. Thus both \(r\) and \(r+6\) are prime, and \(r>N\).

Because \(N\) was arbitrary, prime pairs at distance six occur with first member above every bound. Hence there are infinitely many pairs \((r,r+6)\) of primes.

We have proved, from the stated positivity hypothesis for \(A219055\), Goldbach's conjecture, Lemoine's conjecture, and the infinitude of prime pairs \((p,p+6)\), as required.
